params.question: A 55-year-old man has anaemia with a mean corpuscular volume of 108 fL and a reticulocyte production index of 0.9. Using the two-axis classification framework, which diagnosis does this profile most strongly support?

answers.text: Acute blood loss with a reactive marrow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acute blood loss produces a normocytic anaemia (MCV 80–100 fL) and, after a day or two, a high reticulocyte production index as the marrow responds briskly. An MCV of 108 fL excludes this pattern.

answers.text: Iron deficiency anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron deficiency produces a microcytic anaemia (MCV <80 fL), not a macrocytic one. Red cells are small because haem synthesis is limited by iron lack — the MCV here is in the opposite direction.

answers.text: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A macrocytic MCV (>100 fL) combined with a low reticulocyte production index (<2) is the hallmark of megaloblastic anaemia. Impaired DNA synthesis allows cells to grow but not divide, producing large red cells while marrow output remains insufficient.

answers.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hereditary spherocytosis is a haemolytic anaemia. It typically shows a normal or mildly reduced MCV and a high reticulocyte production index (≥2) as the marrow compensates for ongoing red cell destruction — the opposite RPI pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: Use both axes together. MCV >100 fL indicates macrocytic anaemia; RPI <2 confirms the marrow is underperforming. Together they point to B12 or folate deficiency, not a haemolytic or microcytic cause.
Correct. Macrocytic MCV (>100 fL) plus hypoproliferative RPI (<2) defines megaloblastic anaemia — the marrow cannot respond because DNA synthesis is blocked by B12 or folate deficiency.

interactions.label: A 50-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis has a haemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL and

params.question: A 50-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis has a haemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL and normocytic red cells. Which laboratory profile is most consistent with anaemia of chronic disease rather than iron deficiency anaemia?

answers.text: Low serum ferritin, elevated total iron-binding capacity, transferrin saturation below 16%

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the classic iron deficiency anaemia pattern — depleted stores drive ferritin down and TIBC up as the body upregulates transferrin synthesis. Anaemia of chronic disease operates through a fundamentally different mechanism.

answers.text: Normal or elevated serum ferritin, low total iron-binding capacity, normocytic red cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In anaemia of chronic disease, interleukin-6 stimulates hepcidin, which traps iron inside macrophages. Ferritin — an acute-phase reactant — rises even as functional iron is unavailable to the marrow. TIBC falls because transferrin synthesis is suppressed. The anaemia is normocytic in about three quarters of cases.

answers.text: Low serum ferritin, elevated red cell distribution width, pencil cells on the peripheral smear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pencil cells, elevated RDW, and low ferritin form the fingerprint of iron deficiency anaemia. Tuberculosis can cause both ACD and IDA, but the hepcidin-mediated trapping pattern of ACD differs fundamentally from true iron depletion.

answers.text: High transferrin saturation, elevated ferritin, and ring sideroblasts on marrow examination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: High transferrin saturation with ring sideroblasts is the pattern of sideroblastic anaemia, where iron loads into mitochondria but cannot be incorporated into haem. This is distinct from both IDA and anaemia of chronic disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key differentiator is ferritin: it is low in iron deficiency anaemia and normal or elevated in anaemia of chronic disease, because in ACD the problem is iron trapping by hepcidin, not iron depletion.
Correct. In ACD, hepcidin traps iron in macrophages: ferritin rises as an acute-phase protein, TIBC falls, and the anaemia is typically normocytic — the opposite of the IDA profile.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old male farmworker presents with fatigue and pallor. His haemoglobin

params.question: A 45-year-old male farmworker presents with fatigue and pallor. His haemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic red cells. Which combination of history domains is most essential to determine the aetiology of his anaemia?

answers.text: Family history of haemoglobinopathy and dietary history alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Family history and dietary iron intake are relevant, but in a middle-aged male farmworker they are insufficient. Gastrointestinal blood loss — including occult malignancy — and occupational hookworm exposure are higher-yield domains that must not be omitted.

answers.text: Gastrointestinal bleeding history, dietary history, and occupational exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In an adult male with microcytic anaemia, gastrointestinal bleeding must be excluded first, including the possibility of malignancy. Dietary deficiency of haem iron is common. Barefoot farm work is the key occupational exposure for hookworm infestation — a major driver of iron deficiency anaemia in rural India.

answers.text: Menstrual history and prior medications

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Menstrual history is a high-yield domain for women of reproductive age, where menorrhagia is a leading cause of iron deficiency anaemia in Indian women. It is not applicable to a male patient. Medications are relevant but not the priority in this presentation.

answers.text: Pica history and prior illness only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pica reliably flags iron deficiency and prior illness matters, but neither alone constitutes the most critical combination for a male farmworker. Gastrointestinal bleeding and hookworm exposure are the domains that most sharply prioritise the differential in this context.

overallFeedback.feedback: In adult males, menstrual history is irrelevant. Focus on gastrointestinal bleeding including occult malignancy, dietary haem-iron sources, and occupational hookworm exposure — the three domains that most sharply narrow the differential for microcytic anaemia in a male farmworker.
Correct. For a male patient with microcytic anaemia, gastrointestinal blood loss, dietary iron intake, and barefoot farm work (hookworm exposure) are the three most yield-generating history domains.

params.question: A 32-year-old pregnant woman has a haemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 106 fL. Her serum homocysteine is markedly elevated, but serum methylmalonic acid is within normal limits. Which diagnosis does this metabolic pattern most specifically indicate?

answers.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vitamin B12 deficiency elevates both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. A normal methylmalonic acid level effectively excludes B12 deficiency as the primary cause, because MMA is the most specific confirmatory marker for B12 — it rises only when B12-dependent metabolism is impaired.

answers.text: Folate deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Folate deficiency raises homocysteine because folate is required for the conversion of homocysteine to methionine. However, methylmalonic acid metabolism depends on B12, not folate, so MMA remains normal. Elevated homocysteine with normal MMA therefore points specifically to folate deficiency.

answers.text: Iron deficiency anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron deficiency anaemia is microcytic (MCV <80 fL) and does not affect homocysteine or methylmalonic acid. A macrocytic MCV of 106 fL with elevated homocysteine indicates impaired DNA synthesis — a feature of B-vitamin deficiency, not iron metabolism.

answers.text: Anaemia of chronic disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anaemia of chronic disease is typically normocytic (MCV 80–100 fL) and does not elevate homocysteine or methylmalonic acid. The macrocytic MCV and the metabolic marker pattern here clearly indicate a deficiency of a B-vitamin involved in DNA synthesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Both B12 and folate deficiency raise homocysteine. The discriminator is methylmalonic acid: it rises only in B12 deficiency. A normal MMA with elevated homocysteine therefore points to folate, not B12.
Correct. Elevated homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid is the functional signature of folate deficiency — MMA rises only when B12-dependent metabolism is disrupted.

interactions.label: A 28-year-old vegetarian woman has a haemoglobin of 7.6 g/dL, a mean corpuscular

params.question: A 28-year-old vegetarian woman has a haemoglobin of 7.6 g/dL, a mean corpuscular volume of 110 fL, and macro-ovalocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils on the peripheral smear. A colleague proposes prescribing folic acid 5 mg daily immediately, without first checking vitamin B12 levels. Why is this approach potentially dangerous?

answers.text: Folic acid competes with vitamin B12 for intestinal absorption and will worsen B12 stores

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Folate and B12 use entirely separate absorption mechanisms — intrinsic factor for B12 in the terminal ileum, and folate-specific transporters for dietary folate in the proximal small intestine. There is no direct competition at the absorption level.

answers.text: Folic acid corrects the blood count but allows subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord to progress silently

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the folic acid trap. If the underlying cause is B12 deficiency, folate normalises haematopoiesis and the haemoglobin rises — masking the diagnosis. However, demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord continues unchecked and can become irreversible. B12 status must be confirmed before folate is prescribed alone.

answers.text: Folic acid supplementation is contraindicated during the first trimester of pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The opposite is true. Folic acid 400 micrograms daily is recommended periconceptionally and throughout the first trimester to prevent neural tube defects. High-dose folic acid is also used safely in confirmed folate deficiency.

answers.text: High-dose folate causes thrombocytosis, which increases the risk of venous thromboembolism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Folic acid does not cause thrombocytosis. The danger of giving folate without checking B12 is entirely neurological: it masks the haematological abnormality of B12 deficiency while spinal cord degeneration advances.

overallFeedback.feedback: The folic acid trap: folate corrects the blood picture in B12 deficiency, but subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord progresses silently and can become irreversible. Always check vitamin B12 levels first.
Correct. Always exclude B12 deficiency before prescribing folate alone — folate relieves the anaemia but cannot prevent or reverse B12-mediated subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.
